paragraphs.text: Congenital prothrombin (factor II) deficiency is among the rarest inherited coagulation disorders. Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009) distinguished 2 main phenotypes: hypoprothrombinemia (type I deficiency), with low levels of both activity and antigen, and dysprothrombinemia (type II deficiency), with normal or near-normal synthesis of a dysfunctional protein. In some compound heterozygotes, hypoprothrombinemia occurs together with dysprothrombinemia. Meeks and Abshire (2008) reported that low prothrombin activity typically prolongs both the activated partial thromboplastin time and the prothrombin time, and that bleeding is mainly mucosal or associated with surgery or trauma, although joint bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage have been reported.

paragraphs.text: Owen et al. (1978) separated inherited prothrombin defects into hypoprothrombinemia, a significant reduction of the plasma protein, and dysprothrombinemia, a functionally abnormal prothrombin. Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009) called these type I and type II deficiency, respectively. Individual dysfunctional variants were named after the place where they were found, for example prothrombin Barcelona (Josso et al., 1971), Padua (Girolami et al., 1974), Quick (Owen et al., 1978), Houston (Weinger et al., 1980), and Gainesville (Smith et al., 1981).

paragraphs.text: Shapiro et al. (1969) studied a large family in which 11 members had half-normal plasma levels of biologic prothrombin activity but normal amounts of immunoreactive prothrombin. Prothrombin purified from 1 affected person gave normal protein yields but half-normal activity. When activated, it produced half or less of the thrombin clotting and esterase activity expected from normal prothrombin. Immunoelectrophoresis of serum showed a normal nonthrombin 'pro piece' and an extra activation product. The authors concluded that affected people were heterozygotes in whom half of the prothrombin molecules were structurally abnormal and could not release active thrombin. They called the disorder congenital dysprothrombinemia.

paragraphs.text: Weinger et al. (1980) described prothrombin Houston in a 72-year-old man who had bruised easily and bled after trauma all his life. His prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were prolonged, as were his Stypven, Taipan, and Echis carinatus venom clotting times. Plasma prothrombin coagulant activity was low relative to prothrombin antigen. On crossed immunoelectrofocusing, the patient's prothrombin antigen was more basic than normal. Prothrombin eluted from his plasma was cleaved by Echis carinatus venom but clotted purified fibrinogen more slowly than normal eluate. The authors concluded that the disorder resulted from the generation of a dysfunctional thrombin.
